ch22.title: The Empty Tomb and Peter Forgiven
ch22.b002: Early on Sunday morning the ten apostles lay asleep on the couches of the upper room, the very couches on which they had reclined three days before at their last supper with the Master. It was less sleep than the collapse of exhausted men. Thomas’s place was empty. He had shown his face for a few minutes the night before, and then had gone out without a word. And there was one more empty place, the place at the Master’s left. No one wanted to look that way.
ch22.b003: Even in his sleep Peter could smell charcoal. His dreams always took him back to the same place: the courtyard of Annas, the chill of the night, the servants standing around the fire, and the words coming out of his own mouth. I do not know the man. Over and over. Each time he said it, he wished it were not his voice. But it was his voice. And afterward the Master, passing along the porch, had turned his head and looked at him. There had been no reproach in that look. That was what hurt most. He had sat down by the road and wept. Waking did not stop the weeping.
ch22.b004: Downstairs someone was pounding on the door, hard and urgent. All ten sat up at once. Had the men of the Sanhedrin come for them? James Zebedee froze halfway to his feet; the twins clutched each other’s arms. But it was women who came up the stairs: Mary Magdalene; Salome, the mother of the Zebedee brothers; Joanna, the wife of Chuza; Susanna, the daughter of Ezra of Alexandria; and Mary, the mother of the Alpheus twins. A little before three that morning they had set out for the tomb laden with ointments and linen bandages. Now their faces held terror, and something else mixed with it.
ch22.b005: The women all spoke at once. The stone had been rolled away. The tomb was empty. And they had seen the Master; they had talked with him. The apostles looked at one another. None of them believed it. The women, crushed by grief, had seen some vision in the half-dark of dawn; that was what they thought. Then Mary Magdalene stepped forward. She steadied her breath and repeated the Master’s words just as he had spoken them: they were to go and tell his apostles, and Peter, that he had risen.
ch22.b006: And Peter. Peter heard it. It was his own name. He did not think anything at all. His body moved first. He was down the stairs at a run, and close behind him came another pair of feet. It was John.
ch22.b007: The twins stayed where they were. Their mother was there. She looked at her sons. James Alpheus went to her and took her hand. It was cold, from the dawn air or from something else, he could not tell. She said nothing. But hers were not the eyes of someone telling a lie. The twins had grown up looking into those eyes. The women told their story over again to the other apostles. The others still did not believe, and they did not run to the tomb to see.
ch22.b009: The two of them raced north through the lanes of the city. In Peter’s chest fear and hope surged up by turns. He was afraid to meet the Master. If he did, with what face would he stand before him? But that one phrase, and Peter, drove him forward. As he ran, he suddenly remembered that the Master had said he would rise on the third day. It was a strange thing. From Friday morning until now that promise had not once come into his head. Only now, running toward the Damascus gate with his breath rasping in his throat, did it come back to him.
ch22.b010: John pulled ahead. John was young. Peter at thirty-four could not keep up with John at twenty-eight. John’s back drew farther and farther away, and Peter ran with his eyes on it. It was the back of the one man who had stayed to the end on Friday. It was right that he should reach the tomb first, Peter thought, gasping.
ch22.b011: Joseph’s tomb lay in his garden on the hillside to the east of the road. The great stone at its mouth had been rolled aside along its groove. John stood at the entrance, looking in, but he did not enter. Peter came up panting. He did not stop. He stooped and went straight in. The light from the eastern sky dimly lit the inside of the tomb. On the stone shelf where the body had lain were the bandages, lying just as they had been wound, as though no hand had touched them. Where the head had rested lay the folded napkin. The covering sheet lay at the foot of the niche. Only the body was gone.
ch22.b012: When Peter came out, John went in. He too looked for a long time. Then the two of them sat down on a stone near the entrance. The morning birds were starting to sing in the trees of the garden. Peter spoke first.
ch22.b013: “Someone has robbed the grave. They might have bribed the guards.”
ch22.b014: John shook his head. If thieves had taken the body, he said, the tomb would never have been left so orderly. And how could the bandages have stayed where they were, like that? Peter had no answer. They went back in and examined the grave cloths more closely. The bandages lay as if the body inside them had simply vanished from that very place.
ch22.b015: John stood looking down at them for a long time. On Friday afternoon he had carried that body, wrapped in linen, on his own shoulder to this tomb. He could still feel the weight of it. And now the bandages were empty. Something rose quietly in John’s heart. It was still too frightened to be called joy, and already too large to be called hope. Of all the twelve, John was the first to believe, really and fully, that the Master had risen. That belief began here, in this tomb, before the folded napkin.
ch22.b016: Peter fixed the sight in his mind. All that day, and for a long time afterward, he could not shake it off.
ch22.b017: When they came out the second time, someone was weeping at the mouth of the tomb. It was Mary Magdalene. When the apostles would not believe her, she had lost heart and come back here, wanting to be near the place where she had heard the Master’s voice. Peter and John did not know what to say to her. They left her there and went back into the city. Only when they reached the upper room did they learn that after they had gone the Master had appeared to her again. Mary had run back ahead of them and told it once more, and once more no one had believed her. But when the two who had seen the empty tomb came in, the mockery stopped. Their faces put an end to it. In its place, fear filled the room.
ch22.b019: Before the morning was far along, David Zebedee and Joseph of Arimathea climbed the stairs to the upper room. They too had come from the tomb. They had heard the women’s report, hurried out, and found everything as the women had said. They sat down with the ten apostles and talked with them. But the thinking in the room leaned mostly one way: the Jews had removed the body. Only John was inclined to believe, even faintly, that the Master had risen. Peter had believed while he ran to the tomb; but when he did not find the Master there, he sank back into deep doubt.
ch22.b020: David did not argue with them. As he rose to go, he told them that they were the apostles, and ought to understand these things. He would not dispute with them. But he had heard the Master say that he would rise on the third day, and he believed him; and now he was going back to the house of Nicodemus to send out his waiting messengers on their last errand, to carry the news of the resurrection. He walked toward the stairs, and beside Matthew Levi he stopped. He let a heavy leather bag drop into Matthew’s lap. He said nothing. Then he went down.
ch22.b021: Matthew looked at the bag in his lap. He knew it. For three years it had hung at Judas Iscariot’s waist. All the funds of the apostles were in it. Matthew could not bring himself to grasp it. He felt the leather might still be warm. He knew how much of the money that had gone into that bag had come out of his own pocket, given quietly in the names of other believers so that no one would know. Now that money had gone round and round and come back to his lap, in a bag that had no keeper.
ch22.b022: That day Matthew listened to his fellows talk. But while his ears heard their words, his mind was busy with other figures. What would ten men, no, eleven, eat next week? Judas was gone. David had handed over the money without any ceremony and left. There was no one with authority to lead them. Risen or not risen, men have to eat. It was the sort of thing Philip had always said. Only now did Matthew understand it. And he found that while he was reckoning, he could forget his grief. The thought flickered across his mind that perhaps Judas had been the same. Matthew pushed that thought away quickly.
ch22.b024: It was a long day. They barred the doors and spent most of it in the upper room. They could have slipped out of the city, but they were afraid of being caught abroad by agents of the Sanhedrin. Now and then John Mark came up with news from around the temple and the rumors in the streets. But it did not occur to him to gather reports from the various groups of believers who claimed to have seen the Master. That had always been the work of David’s messengers, and the messengers were all far away now on their last errand. For the first time the apostles realized how much they had leaned on those runners for their daily knowledge of things.
ch22.b025: So they knew nothing of what happened that day. That about noon, in the garden of Lazarus at Bethany, the Master had appeared to James, his eldest brother. That shortly before two o’clock, in the home of Martha and Mary, his family and their friends, twenty in all, had seen him. That a little after four, the women gathered at the house of Joseph of Arimathea had seen him, and a little later the Greek believers gathered at the house of Flavius. All over the city people were beginning to say they had seen him. Only the ten who had followed him longest sat behind a locked door, waiting. The Master had not forgotten them. He was giving them time to turn over everything he had told them while he was with them in the flesh. And he was waiting for Peter to fight his own particular battle through first. The ten knew nothing of that.
ch22.b026: Andrew mostly listened that day. He was bewildered. He had doubts, more than his share of them. That the tomb was empty was a fact. But an empty tomb proved nothing. What was it the women had seen? Andrew was a judge of men. He could tell what a man saw from what a man wanted to see. But today that eye could tell him nothing. Only one thing surprised him: his shoulders felt light. Before these confused days came, the Master had released him from the leadership of the apostles. Andrew was strangely grateful that he was not the one who had to lead these ten men now. And he was a little ashamed of being grateful.
ch22.b027: All day John held on to one thought: the Master had risen. Counting on his fingers, he went through every time the Master had said he would rise again. There were more than five. At least three times he had spoken of the third day. John’s words moved his brother James and Nathaniel a good deal. They would have moved more of the others if John had not been the youngest. At first James Zebedee had insisted they all go out to the tomb together; they had to do something to get to the bottom of this. Nathaniel stopped him, reminding them of the Master’s warning not to risk their lives needlessly at such a time. By noon James had subsided. He hardly spoke. It disappointed him bitterly that the Master did not show himself to them.
ch22.b028: Through those long, weary hours it was Nathaniel who held the ten together. Now and then, in a low voice, he would set out his thoughts: a man should not rush in the face of what he does not understand; waiting is also a kind of work. He never once said whether he believed in the resurrection or not. But as the day wore on, what he said leaned, little by little, in one direction. The Master was one who kept his promises.
ch22.b029: Simon Zelotes lay on a couch in a corner with his face to the wall. All day he did not speak half a dozen times. His kingdom had fallen. Even the news of the empty tomb could not set it up again. If the man had risen, what difference did it make? Rome was still there. His disappointment was too deep and too much his own to be reached by anyone else’s news. If someone laid a hand on his shoulder, he neither shrank from it nor welcomed it.
ch22.b030: Philip, usually so quiet, was oddly talkative that afternoon. He kept asking the others questions. If the Master had really risen, what would he look like? Above all, would his body still bear the marks of the cross? Peter was often irritated by the questions. The others put up with them good-naturedly. Philip had always been a man who had to see in order to know. Today he spent the hours asking about what could not be seen.
ch22.b032: The twins took little part in the serious talk. They were busy with what they always did. They fetched water, shared out bread, cleared the empty bowls, filled the lamps with oil. They were the men who had managed the crowds. With no crowd now, they managed the crowd of ten. They knew who had not eaten and who had not drunk. It was they who set a piece of bread and a cup of water by Simon Zelotes’s head. Simon did not touch it. Toward evening the twins took away the untouched bread and put down fresh.
ch22.b033: Late in the afternoon Philip asked them what they made of all this. The twins looked at each other. One of them answered, and he answered for both.
ch22.b034: “We don’t know what this rising from the dead is. But our mother says she spoke with the Master, and we believe our mother.”
ch22.b035: Philip looked at them for a long moment. He asked nothing more. The twins went back to clearing the bowls. They were the only apostles who had not finished the synagogue school. They had understood half of the Master’s deeper sayings, sometimes less. But they knew how to trust a person. With them, trust came before understanding. They believed their mother the same way they had always believed the Master. They believed without knowing, and because they believed, they followed.
ch22.b036: Their mother Mary had been one of the five women who went to the tomb at dawn. She was an ordinary woman who had borne and raised the twins in a fishing village near Kheresa. What she had seen, her sons had not seen. But Judas Alpheus thought: it is enough that our mother saw. Someday we will see. And if we never see, that is all right too. The thought did not trouble him in the least. While the other eight swung all day between doubt and fear, the twins alone stayed in one place. No one in the room noticed it. They did not notice it themselves. Looking back, though, after John it was these twins who first believed in the Master’s resurrection. The two who understood least believed first. Through the night of the trial, the day of the cross, and the Sabbath of despair, they had never once let go of their heart’s faith in him. They simply did not know to call it faith.
ch22.b038: No one was shaken that day as hard as Peter. He believed, then doubted, then doubted and believed again. When he closed his eyes he saw the grave cloths in the tomb, the bandages lying as though the body had evaporated from inside them. He could not explain it. Then why? He chewed over the question again and again. If the Master had really risen and could show himself to the women, why did he not come to his apostles? Only one answer came to him. Because of me. Because the man who denied him is in this room, he does not come.
ch22.b039: Each time that thought came, he could hardly breathe. And he thought of Judas, the man whose end had come in the valley of Hinnom. Peter shuddered. Had he not betrayed the Master too? He had taken no silver, but by the charcoal fire, had he not handed over the Master to buy his own life? He did not know whether he was still an apostle. Perhaps he was not one anymore. Then he would cling again to that one phrase. And Peter. If those were truly the Master’s words, then the Master had not cast him off. But to believe the words, he had to believe that the women had truly seen the Master. All day he swung between the two.
ch22.b040: A little after eight in the evening he made up his mind. Without telling anyone, he went down the stairs and out into the garden. He ought to take himself out of that room, he thought, so that the Master would not be kept from his brethren on his account. The garden of the Mark home stood dark with flowers and shrubs. The April night air carried the scent of blossoms. Peter walked slowly among them.
ch22.b041: He thought of the look the Master had given him as he passed along the porch of Annas’s house. There had been no reproach in it. There had been love. Since dawn on Friday he had been avoiding that look, because he could not bear the love in it. Now he faced it squarely. And once more he turned over the message the women had brought. And Peter. When he set the two side by side, something turned over inside him. They were tokens of mercy, both of them. His faith began to rise above his doubts. He stopped walking. He clenched both fists. And he spoke aloud.
ch22.b042: “He has risen. I believe it. I will go and tell my brothers.”
ch22.b043: Before the words were finished, a man’s form stood in front of him. And a familiar voice spoke his name.
ch22.b044: Peter could not move. The Master told him that the enemy had wanted him, but he had not given him up. He had known, he said, that it was not from the heart that Peter had disowned him, and so he had forgiven him even before he asked.
ch22.b045: The strength went out of Peter’s legs. Before he asked. He had not yet asked for anything. For three days he had not once prayed for it, because he did not know what words to use. And yet forgiveness was already there. It had been there even at the moment when, beside the charcoal fire, he denied the Master for the last time; perhaps even before that.
ch22.b046: The Master went on. Peter must now stop thinking about himself and the troubles of this hour, he said, and get ready to carry the good news to those who sat in darkness. He should no longer care what he might gain from the kingdom, but should put his strength into what he could give to those who were desperately poor in spirit. And calling him Simon, he told him to gird himself for the battle of a new day, the struggle against the spiritual darkness and the evil doubtings in the minds of men.
ch22.b047: They walked through the garden together for nearly five minutes, talking of things past, present, and to come. Afterward Peter could not remember all that he had said in those minutes. He knew only that he had been walking side by side with the Master, as he had walked with him on the shore at Capernaum and along the roads of Galilee. At the end the Master bade him farewell until he should see him again with his brethren. And he vanished from before Peter’s eyes.
ch22.b048: Peter stood there for a while. The scent of the flowers came back. He knew that he had spoken with the risen Master. He knew that he was still an ambassador of the kingdom. Three years before, by the fire in the garden of Zebedee’s house, he had sworn he would not turn back. That vow had broken beside the charcoal fire in the courtyard of Annas. Yet the Master had not thrown the broken vow away. He had picked it up, brought it back, and put it into Peter’s hands again. Peter drew a long breath. Then he ran for the stairs.
ch22.b050: Peter pushed open the door of the upper room. He was out of breath. All ten faces turned toward him at once.
ch22.b051: “I’ve seen the Master! He was in the garden. He talked with me. He has forgiven me.”
ch22.b052: A stir went through the room. Peter’s face said that this was no lie. The apostles were deeply moved. They were on the point of laying their doubts aside. Then Andrew stood up.
ch22.b053: Andrew warned the brethren not to be carried away by his brother’s report. Peter, he said, had seen things before that were not real. He did not mention outright the night on the Sea of Galilee, when Peter had claimed to see the Master walking toward the boat on the water. But he said enough that everyone in the room knew what he meant.
ch22.b054: The light went out of Peter’s face. He looked at his brother. He said nothing. He drew back to one side of the room, sat down, and sank into silence. What he had been given in the garden was still inside him. But he had no strength to bring it out and show it again. These were his own brother’s words.
ch22.b055: Andrew sat down again. He knew what he had said. He knew too how much it had hurt his brother. And still he believed he had to say it. Or he believed he believed it. He was a man who did not speak of what he was not sure of. And he was a man who did not take another man’s certainty for his own. That was his way. Many times that way had kept the group safe. But tonight he caught a faint glimpse of what lay behind it. His brother had always believed before he did. Spoke first, leaped first, wept first. And today he had seen first. Andrew did not envy him for it. He had never been jealous of Peter. Only, when his brother said he had seen what Andrew had not seen, Andrew did not know how to believe him. A mouth that could not give praise could not give trust either.
ch22.b056: Then the twins got up, both together. They crossed the room to Peter. Judas Alpheus sat down on one side of him, James on the other. They felt so sorry for him that they could not bear it. They did not know how to comfort him. So they said what they knew.
ch22.b058: “Our mother saw the Master too. What you saw was the Master.”
ch22.b059: Peter raised his head. The twins’ faces were alike. Alike in their simplicity, alike in their earnestness. They did not know what rising from the dead was. They did not know what had happened in the garden. But they believed Peter. Peter looked from one face to the other and laughed, a laugh with tears in it. Three years before, on the night of the ordination, the twins had fallen asleep by the fire while the others went in one by one to talk with the Master and hear him. That night the Master had said not to wake them; they were doing well. Peter remembered that night. And he knew who in this room tonight was doing best of all.
ch22.b060: Nathaniel went over beside Andrew. He spoke to him in a low voice. It was less a rebuke than a quiet remonstrance. Andrew bowed his head and listened.
ch22.b062: At about nine o’clock there were hurried footsteps on the stairs again. It was the two brothers from Emmaus, Cleopas and Jacob. They burst into the room, crying out that they had seen Jesus and talked with him. That afternoon, they said, on the road to Emmaus, a stranger had walked along with them. He had opened the Scriptures to them, and only when they reached their house and he broke the bread did they know who he was. They had not stayed to eat; they had come straight back to Jerusalem. When they had finished their story they soon left.
ch22.b063: The room boiled up again. The women; Cleopas and Jacob; and Peter. Now there were three separate accounts of seeing the Master. Yet of the ten, no one but Peter had seen him. The twins still sat on either side of Peter, comforting him. Nathaniel was still remonstrating with Andrew. Every door was bolted for fear of arrest.
ch22.b064: Then it happened. The Master was standing in their midst. The door had not opened. No one had heard a step on the stairs. He was there.
ch22.b065: First he wished them peace. Then he asked why they were so frightened, as if they were looking at a spirit. Had he not told them about all this while he was with them in the flesh? That the chief priests and rulers would hand him over to be killed, that one of their own number would betray him, and that on the third day he would rise? Why, then, all this doubting, all this arguing over the reports of the women, of Cleopas and Jacob, and even of Peter? How long would they doubt his words and refuse to trust his promises? And now that they saw him with their own eyes, would they believe?
ch22.b066: Even of Peter. Andrew went rigid at those words. The Master did not look at him. He did not rebuke him. He only set Peter’s name beside the names of the women and the brothers from Emmaus, among those who had seen and told. Andrew understood well enough from that.
ch22.b067: The Master went on. Even now, he said, one of them was missing. When they were all together again, and all of them knew for certain that the Son of Man had risen from the grave, they were to leave and go into Galilee. They should have faith in God, and faith in one another; so they would enter the new service of the kingdom of heaven. He would stay in Jerusalem with them until they were ready to go into Galilee. He left them his peace.
ch22.b068: And in an instant he was gone from their sight.
ch22.b069: No one spoke. They all fell on their faces. They praised God. They worshiped the Master who had just vanished. Simon Zelotes was down from his couch and on his face with the rest; no one had seen when he came down. Matthew lay with his forehead on the floor, Judas’s bag set down before his knees. Philip, face down, thought: I did not see the marks. He came too suddenly and went too suddenly. But that night, for the first time, he did not want to ask.
ch22.b070: How long it was, no one could say. Andrew was the first to rise. He crossed the room to his brother. Peter still lay face down. Andrew knelt beside him. He had to say something. That he was sorry; that Peter had been right. But again those words hung somewhere in his throat. He reached out and laid his hand on his brother’s shoulder, as he had by the fire in the garden three years before. Peter lifted his head and looked at him. Neither brother said a word. Peter put his own hand over his brother’s. It was enough. The words Andrew could not say that night were still inside him. Someday the day would come to say them.
ch22.b072: The next day they did not leave. The day after that, they did not leave either. The Master’s words, that one of them was missing, held them there. John Mark had already told them on Sunday morning that Thomas was at the house of Simon in Bethpage. If any two of them had gone that day and asked him to come back, Thomas would have come. But no one went. The apostles waited for Thomas to return, and Thomas waited for them to come for him. And so a week went by.
ch22.b073: That week Peter was changed. He was still talkative. He was still hasty. But now there was weight in what he said. The words he had heard in the garden were growing in him. Stop thinking about yourself. He said it over to himself again and again. For three days he had thought of nothing but himself: his shame, his sin, whether he was still an apostle. Now he began to think of others. Of Simon Zelotes lying with his face to the wall; of Matthew with Judas’s bag in his lap; and of Thomas, who must be wandering alone over the hills.
ch22.b074: On Monday morning Andrew sat by the window turning over the Master’s words of the night before. Have faith in God; have faith in one another. Faith in God he was sure of. It was the second part that was hard. Faith in one another. He knew the twelve better than anyone. He knew each man’s weaknesses, what shook him, what he feared. But knowing a man and trusting him were not the same. He had known his brother’s weakness so well that he could not trust what his brother had seen. He had seen what was stirring in Judas and still had not gone to him. That morning, for the first time, Andrew wondered whether the eye that knew men had been tying the hand that should have trusted them.
ch22.b075: That week Mary, the Master’s mother, spent much of her time with the women believers at the house of Joseph of Arimathea. On Tuesday, far off at Philadelphia, about a hundred and fifty believers led by Abner and Lazarus saw the Master. Early the next morning they set out, proclaiming that Jesus of Nazareth had risen from the dead. Believers far away had already taken to the roads with the news, while the men who had been nearest the Master the longest were still waiting for one brother. The apostles knew nothing of what had happened at Philadelphia. Even if they had known, they would not have left. The Master had told them to gather together, all of them.
ch22.b076: Andrew and Peter did not talk much that week. But they always sat near each other. At meals Andrew would put bread in his brother’s bowl first. Peter noticed it. It was his brother’s apology. All his life his brother had done things that way instead of saying them. For the first time, Peter received his brother’s way gratefully.
ch22.b077: On Saturday evening darkness came down. Peter stood up.
ch22.b079: No one in the room was surprised. Perhaps they had all been waiting for him to say it. John took up a lamp and rose to go with him. The two of them went down the stairs and out into the dark streets. They were the two who had run together to the tomb at dawn a week before. This time they did not run. The way to Bethpage, toward the Mount of Olives, was dark, and as he walked Peter thought. A week ago he had tried to take himself away from his brothers, afraid that because of him the Master would not come. Now he was going to fetch a brother who had taken himself away. The way the Master had come for him. Before he asked.
ch22.b081: The course of events follows Papers 189–191. The ten apostles asleep in the upper room and Thomas’s absence (189:4.1); the names of the five women and their visit to the tomb, their report and the words “and Peter,” Peter and John running to the tomb, the promise of the third day coming back to Peter only then, John arriving first and looking in while Peter entered first, the arrangement of the grave cloths and the two men’s discussion, and Mary Magdalene weeping at the tomb (189:4.3–5.5); the visit of David and Joseph, John alone inclined to believe, and David dropping Judas’s bag of funds into Matthew’s lap (190:1.2–1.3); the apostles through resurrection Sunday (191:0.1–0.13); the appearance to Peter in the garden and his forgiveness, Andrew’s warning and the twins’ comfort, and the appearance to the ten (191:1.1–2.2); the other appearances that day, unknown to the apostles (190:2.2–4.2); the report of Cleopas and Jacob (190:5.8); the appearance at Philadelphia that week and where the Master’s mother stayed (191:4.1–4.6, 192:0.3); and the week of waiting, with Peter and John going on Saturday evening to bring Thomas back (191:0.13, 191:4.6, 191:5.1). The denial in Annas’s courtyard and the Master’s look follow 184:2.
ch22.b082: Character details come from Paper 139: the twins the only apostles who were not graduates of the synagogue schools (139:0.3); their simple faith and their being the first, after John, to believe in the resurrection (139:9.2–9.11); John the first really and fully to believe in the resurrection (139:4.10); Andrew’s reluctance to praise and his freedom from jealousy of Peter (139:1.6, 139:1.10); Matthew secretly making up the apostolic funds (139:7.8–7.9); and the disappointment of Simon Zelotes (139:11). The twins asleep on the night of the ordination and the pledge in the garden come from 140:6.
ch22.b083: Added as fiction are the inner thoughts and memories of Peter, Andrew, the twins, and Matthew; the scenery of the garden and the dawn streets; the twins leaving bread by Simon Zelotes’s head and James Alpheus taking his mother’s hand; Andrew’s hand on his brother’s shoulder and the bread he set in Peter’s bowl through the week; and Peter’s brief words on Saturday evening. Peter’s words at the tomb and in the garden, his report in the upper room, and the twins’ answer follow the sense of the text in other words; the twins’ comforting words to Peter put the content of the text into dialogue. The gestures of Simon Zelotes, Matthew, Philip, and Andrew after the appearance to the ten are fiction.
ch22.b084: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
